doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Popular music, the business takeover and the Grammys
summary: In the 1950s the aim was to play in tune; lawyers made music a business.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: Yeah. In the ‘60s, rock was obviously very prevalent. Did the popular music of the day affect your thinking, your own personal style? © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

During that era when we came up, which was in the ‘50s, in the middle of the ‘50s, fundamentally all we were trying to do man is play in tune. Play some good music and play in tune. That’s basically all we were looking forward to doing. Because you had to — the whole thing just turned lopsided. Saxophone players — the only time they could get a job recording in the studio is they would put some gloves on and play. You know? And that’s pretty bad. You know what kind of sound they’re going to get, right? And that’s all the kind of people that they were recording, were letting record. All of a sudden man, when the CPAs and attorneys took over and made this music into a business, that’s when the change came about. You know? Well just look, what was it this year, last year, the Grammy so-called thing, right?
Man, you know, they won’t even put — they won’t even let the jazz artists have any air time.
Right. Previously awards given out. Do you believe that?

Yeah, I’ve heard this point before and you’re backing up a couple of people who have said that some of the record companies used to be run by musicians. And then that kind of ended and things changed.
Yup. Well it became a business, you know, a super business. And we’re drinking apple juice.
